boundary: Every investigation declaration, study directory with a top-level Markdown lead, and released top-level finding/essay at the frozen commit. Short forms, drafts, checkpoints and raw evidence are excluded.

nodes.title: What AI activity costs the shared internet
When a model finds the bug
Where does a software update go?
LH000 Observing one dispatch end to end
nodes.summary: Harbour's take record for this dispatch held 37 item fields, 23 with a value and 14 null: an observation of what Harbour stored, not of what happened on the host. Two host samples six minutes apart found a close to idle four core container, with load averages of 0.02 and 0.01 and 23 then 21 established IPv4 connections, also observations. That this load belongs mostly to the container's own supervisor processes and this session's harness, not the dispatch's own work, is an interpretation: every top process could be named from its command line, though no idle only baseline was sampled. This dispatch's residue inside the repository, so far, is the new directory studies/LH000/ holding this study. Whether the write-up shapes a later dispatch, such as one answering ticket Q-0002 or I-0002, is a scenario, not yet confirmed.
nodes.label: LH000 Observing one dispatch end to end

nodes.title: When something changes in a small software neighbourhood, where does the change appear next?
nodes.summary: In this neighbourhood the change travelled, and the public record shows where it went but not why. Within the window, four of the nine dependents' repositories came to hold the library's new release, mcp 1.27.0. The earliest record of it is R04's first GitHub commit, 2.1 days after publication, which already held it; the first move visible as a change came 6.2 days after publication. In one case the release went a further step: a dependent's own release, published 22 minutes after its update, pinned it for everyone who installs that dependent (observation and derived measurement, git and Open Source Insights). All four moves are explained by ordinary maintenance: a maintainer's standing habit of pinning each new release, this time 22 minutes before the project's own release, a bulk lockfile refresh, the pinning of another package's dependencies, and a first adoption. No identified bot made any of them, and no maintainer identity is shared with the library (derived measurement; interpretation for "explained").
nodes.label: When something changes in a small software neighbourhood, where does the change appear next?

nodes.title: LH003 Survey of surveys
nodes.summary: Thirty-four candidate observatories were considered; seventeen have a full row in sources.md's included table and seventeen are excluded there with a stated reason, an observation. Of the seventeen included, most see only one of LH F02's layers from one narrow population: repository-event archives and dependency resolvers see residue (changed structure), API-broker rankings and vendor usage reports see activity (inference calls), and vulnerability databases see a specific kind of residue, a disclosed flaw, rather than its exploitation. No source in this reading is classed as observing propagation directly. That is Lighthouse's classification, not an observation about the sources: LH F02 defines propagation as a derived link between an earlier residue record and later activity, not a surface any instrument reads off directly, so under that definition no source could be counted as seeing it. The empirical question is which of these records support identifying and testing such links. A propagation claim has to be built by joining two sources' records and testing the join, which is what LH002 is designed to attempt on a small scale for one such join (a dependency change and a dependent's later change) and what this study does not attempt at all. The strongest supported finding, an interpretation resting on the rows above rather than on any single one, is that these seventeen sources are partial views whose relationships to one another are unmeasured in anything this survey read: each is scoped to its own population (one forge, one broker, one vendor's product tiers in a given report, one company's network), no source read here states how much its population overlaps another's, and this study took no joint sample, so their counts cannot simply be added into a total. Distinct boundaries do not establish little overlap, and the table itself records connections, an observation: Open Source Insights links packages in seven ecosystems to their GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket projects and to OSV advisories; OSV.dev aggregates GitHub Security Advisories, PyPA and RustSec among its upstream sources; GitHub's unreviewed advisories come from the NVD feed and are published in OSV format; NVD enriches records that CVE Numbering Authorities assign (this last per a search summary; see the fourth Finding). Where the populations overlap, and by how much, is a question for a joint sample, not something this reading establishes. What stays invisible, or visible only in part, is specific. No source read here can reliably tell a person's download or code change from an agent's. Cloudflare's AI Crawl Control does attribute crawler traffic to named AI operators, and its page lets a site owner group that traffic by crawler, by operator and by "Category: Analyze crawlers by their purpose or type" (an observation, from notes/R-0001.md's raw read of the page, last updated 23 April 2026); but it covers only crawlers Cloudflare has already identified, and because the category belongs to the crawler rather than to any one request, it cannot say why a particular page was fetched (an interpretation). The conversation figures do not say whether a person or a program was typing. No source states at what layer an AI system operated, and usage that happens off all these particular surfaces goes unseen, for instance direct provider API traffic outside a broker, a private repository, or a deployment that never triggers a public event. The first of those examples holds for the sources as read here; the first review note says later Economic Index reports, which this survey has not read, include one vendor's first-party API traffic.
nodes.label: LH003 Survey of surveys

nodes.title: The xz backdoor, read through Lighthouse's three layers
nodes.summary: A compromised release of xz-utils, a compression library that several Linux distributions link into their ssh server through distribution-specific dependencies (see the last finding), carried a backdoor from a tarball built in February 2024 into several distributions' rolling repositories before anyone recognised it (observation, drawn from the sources in Findings). Reading the case through Lighthouse's three layers: the backdoor's residue, malicious code sitting in two release tarballs, was technically public from 24 February 2024, the day version 5.6.0 was released, but nobody detected it there. What was actually detected, twice, sat in the activity layer: memory-checking errors seen in Red Hat's distributions from 4 March, which the backdoor's author answered with a purported fix on 8 March and a reworked backdoor released as 5.6.1 on 9 March, and then, on 29 March, one engineer's own ssh sessions running measurably slower and burning more CPU than they should, alongside valgrind errors on the same machines, which he traced to liblzma and disclosed the same day (observation, S14 and the timeline reconstruction, as read by R-0001). The second of these is the signal that broke the case. The first was not passed over: it was answered, by the person who had planted the backdoor, with changes that took the symptom away (observation of what S14 and the timeline record; the phrase "took the symptom away" is interpretation). Of the two, only the second maps cleanly onto a surface in LH F02's table, Processing, task wall time; the first is a correctness signal from a memory sanitiser, and F02's activity surfaces, tuned to resource consumption, have no row for it (interpretation). Propagation followed only after disclosure gave residue a name: distributions that had already built the compromised tarball reverted their packages within a day, and the case became a CVE, several advisories and a still-cited timeline within the same week (observation, Findings). No instrument Lighthouse has registered or proposed sat at any of these observation points, and the outward instruments LH F02 already names, GH Archive and Open Source Insights, watch source forges and language package ecosystems, not the Linux distribution package pipelines this case actually propagated through (interpretation). Whether an undetected case of the same kind exists today cannot be answered from this one case; it can only say what made this one detectable, which is not the same thing (interpretation, Limits).
nodes.label: The xz backdoor, read through Lighthouse's three layers

nodes.title: Can any public record connect a software release to its installation?
nodes.summary: Partly, and only as far as the download. PyPI's public download record, read through ClickHouse's copy of it, connects a release to the files fetched from PyPI by version, day, installer and a self-reported CI flag. For mcp 1.27.0 it shows the release taken almost at once: 22.3 per cent of all mcp downloads on its release day, 1,639,539 of 7,351,271, in the nine hours after publication; 48.1 per cent the next day; between 45 and 71 per cent of every day's downloads from then to the window's end; 95,672,297 of the window's 219,899,536 mcp downloads in all (observation and derived measurement). By the time the first of LH002's dependents was seen pinning it, six days after publication, the release had been about half of all downloads for five days. What carried it to the downloaders was install-time resolution of open version ranges, mostly by uv (78.6 per cent of the window's downloads), not the dependents' pins (interpretation).
nodes.label: Can any public record connect a software release to its installation?

nodes.title: Is there a public record of what was installed, past the download?
nodes.summary: Yes, in part: a published container image is a public record of installed state, and it reaches past the download to the installation, though not to a run. Inside each image's layers the installer's own record, a site-packages/mcp-<version>.dist-info directory, says which version of mcp was installed, and the image's configuration says when it was built. For the images read here that record could be read anonymously from the registry without pulling the image, by streaming the image's upper layers and stopping at the directory, between 25 and 211 MB of compressed data per image (observation; data/imagemcp.csv).
nodes.label: Is there a public record of what was installed, past the download?

nodes.title: When a widely used library releases, how much of the software built on it installs the new version because an installer resolved an open range, and how much waits for a maintainer to move a pin or lockfile?
nodes.summary: In this sample, the images that resolve an open range took the new release within days, and the images built from a lockfile or an exact pin took it only when the pin moved. For most of the lockfile and exact-pin repositories that was a month or more after the release, or had not happened by 15 August: of 12 such image repositories, 9 had no pin on the new release within four weeks of it, and the largest group of pin moves, four of the nine found, came within 28 hours of a security advisory published a month after the release rather than in the days after the release itself.
nodes.label: When a widely used library releases, how much of the software built on it installs the new version because an installer resolved an open range, and how much waits for a maintainer to move a pin or lockfile?

nodes.title: When software built on a widely used library pins or locks it, what moves the pin: a new release, or a security advisory fixed by one?
nodes.summary: In this sample, pins and locks moved after both, and neither drew most of them. Across four libraries in the top 50 by downloads (urllib3, cryptography, pyjwt, starlette), 102 kept repository and library pairs held a version below a fix when it was released; 73 moved to the fix or later by 27 September, a median 18.7 days after the release (and, for the 54 that moved after the advisory, a median 10.5 days after it), 28 had not moved and one stopped pinning the library. The rate of moves rose in the two days after the release (8 moves, 4.1 per 100 repository-days) and again in the week after the advisory (8 moves in its first two days, 5.1; 14 in days two to seven, 4.3), against 1.3 to 1.7 per 100 repository-days from the third day after the release to the advisory and in the three weeks after the advisory's first week (derived measurement; data/hazard.csv, figure rates.svg). The release's spell lasted two days: from day two to day seven, stopping at the advisory where it came first, the rate was 1.5. No burst like LH007's appeared: 4 of the 102 moved within a day after the advisory, where LH007 found 6 of 13 mcp projects within 28 hours (observation; LH007 is one library and one evening).
nodes.label: When software built on a widely used library pins or locks it, what moves the pin: a new release, or a security advisory fixed by one?

nodes.title: When a fixed release says in its own notes that it fixes a security flaw, do pinned dependents move to it before the advisory is published, more than they move to a fix released silently?
nodes.summary: In this sample, pinned dependents moved to an announced fix before its advisory at about 1.7 times the pace they moved to a silent one, but the same share of their moves came before the advisory, and the difference rests on few moves in few libraries. Of the 37 fixed releases behind LH008's 68 advisories, 19 said in their own changelog, tag or PyPI description, at or before the release, that they fixed a security flaw, and 18 did not (observation; data/fixclasses.csv). Taking each of LH008's 16 libraries' one event (eight announced, eight silent; seven of each had pinned dependents to follow), 257 repository and event pairs held an affected version when the fix came out, and 173 moved to it by 27 September (derived; data/summarybyclass.csv).
nodes.label: When a fixed release says in its own notes that it fixes a security flaw, do pinned dependents move to it before the advisory is published, more than they move to a fix released silently?

nodes.title: Do pinned dependents move faster before the advisory to fixes whose notes announce a security flaw than to silent ones, when each class has enough libraries that no one or two carry the result?
nodes.summary: The study does not settle the question. Before the advisory, pinned dependents moved to announced fixes at a higher pooled rate than to silent ones under every clock and every restriction tried, but with the library as the unit the brief's classes cannot be told apart under any of them (only the strict class under a clock chosen after the fact reaches p < 0.05; "How many comparisons" below), and under the brief's own clock the pooled lead's uncertainty spans no difference. The top 500 projects gave 43 libraries with a qualifying event, not the 40 or more the design needed: 22 announced and 21 silent, of which 18 announced and 12 silent had pinned dependents to follow (observation; brief.md amendment 1, data/summarybyclass.csv). Their 209 repository and event pairs gave 142 moves by 27 September. Version 0.3 reanalysed the retained evidence after every outcome was known (outcome-aware and post hoc, not preregistered; Findings, "Reanalysis of retained evidence, version 0.3"); the first three bullets are version 0.2's figures, unchanged, with one interval added.
nodes.label: Do pinned dependents move faster before the advisory to fixes whose notes announce a security flaw than to silent ones, when each class has enough libraries that no one or two carry the result?

nodes.title: When one of the most downloaded Python projects releases a new version, does it reach half of the project's downloads within two days as a rule, and how much of its early uptake carries the build-server flag, compared with the release it replaces?
nodes.summary: For some projects, not as a rule, by the brief's convention; and the new release's early downloads carry the build-server flag less often than the old release's on the same days, by about seven percentage points.
nodes.label: When one of the most downloaded Python projects releases a new version, does it reach half of the project's downloads within two days as a rule, and how much of its early uptake carries the build-server flag, compared with the release it replaces?

nodes.title: After a new release of one of the most downloaded Python libraries, what keeps older versions downloaded, and which explanations can the public record rule out: other libraries' version bounds, Pythons the new release no longer supports, or environments rebuilt from frozen lists?
nodes.summary: Pythons the newer releases no longer support are ruled out as the main reason for older downloads as a rule: for 32 of the 37 projects (86.5 per cent, project-resampled 95 per cent interval 75.7 to 97.3), less than half of the downloads on versions older than the release of a month before came from a Python that every newer release excludes, even counting downloads with no Python reported as excluded (derived measurement, on the Python the installer reports). For three projects such downloads are most of the older downloads, the brief's class "accounts for most": boto3 (76.3 to 77.0 per cent), aiobotocore (63.0 to 63.5) and numpy (62.5 to 66.7); the question stays open for pandas and urllib3. That class counts fetches that could not have been of R or later; it does not say why they were of the versions they were. For boto3 and aiobotocore few were at the highest version their Python admits, where a fresh install lands (6.7 and 0.6 per cent; numpy 56.7). Read after version 0.2 was released (post hoc, below), their count-by-version profiles are flat for long runs of versions below each Python's edge (for boto3 on Python 3.9, about a hundred at one level and several hundred at the next), the shape an installer's resolution walk leaves when it fetches each version it tries and rejects; on that reading most of those downloads were versions inspected and discarded, not installed (interpretation, untested). Identified bounds, the requirements that the 500 most downloaded projects declare, are in the brief's class "accounts for most" for four tightly coupled projects: pydantic-core (held by pydantic's exact pin), fsspec (by s3fs), and botocore and s3transfer (by boto3). B is an estimate under the co-fetch assumption, that each fetch of a held dependent version brings one fetch of the project, and the log does not observe that, since it counts each project's fetches separately; so the class says what identified bounds could account for, not what they did. The log's own ratios strain the assumption for botocore and s3transfer, boto3 being fetched 2.94 and 3.88 times as often as they are (7.51 times botocore on Python 3.9), and are most consistent with it for pydantic-core, whose dependent is fetched about as often (1.05 times) and whose older fetches sit largely at the one version pydantic's newest releases pin. Only for pydantic-core do the dependent's current versions carry a large part of the hold (53.2 per cent); for fsspec, botocore and s3transfer the hold comes from s3fs's and boto3's older versions, which moves the question to why those are fetched. On the same assumption, identified bounds are ruled out as the main reason for seven projects; they are undetermined for 26, mostly because requirements the log cannot resolve (extras, platform markers, versions not read) leave the upper estimate near one. Environments rebuilt from frozen lists cannot be counted in the log, as the brief said in advance; 18 of the 37 projects show their trace (most older downloads off every version a fresh install on the identified constraints would land on, and more often flagged CI than new downloads). So for most projects the public record rules out the Python explanation, cannot rule identified bounds in or out, and leaves what remains unmeasured, consistent with frozen lists but not shown to be them.
nodes.label: After a new release of one of the most downloaded Python libraries, what keeps older versions downloaded, and which explanations can the public record rule out: other libraries' version bounds, Pythons the new release no longer supports, or environments rebuilt from frozen lists?

nodes.title: Over the two weeks after LH012's, do the 37 libraries' older shares and Python exclusion hold, how much of each library's downloads falls in its single largest combination of reported fields, and does the flat, walk-like shape of some libraries' older downloads hold?
nodes.summary: The study ran. Its eligibility condition was met: on 2 November 2026 at 15:30 UTC, LH012's coverage query found 1 November 2026 as the last day held for every one of the 37 projects in all five per-day tables, and the preflight of 22 October had already found 21 October, so ClickPy held 12 October well before 31 October. When it first held that day the source cannot say (Method). Every day of both weeks was held for every project, no day was a gap, and W0's totals, read again, equalled LH012's to the download for all 37.
nodes.label: Over the two weeks after LH012's, do the 37 libraries' older shares and Python exclusion hold, how much of each library's downloads falls in its single largest combination of reported fields, and does the flat, walk-like shape of some libraries' older downloads hold?

nodes.title: Below the fifty most downloaded Python projects, does a new newest version reach half of its project's downloads within two days as a rule, and does its share settle by day 2?
nodes.summary: Not as a rule in either band, by the brief's convention; the share of projects whose new releases mostly reached half of downloads within two days falls from the top fifty to each band below it. The share of a new release still settles by day 2 as a rule in band A, and for some projects in band B.
nodes.label: Below the fifty most downloaded Python projects, does a new newest version reach half of its project's downloads within two days as a rule, and does its share settle by day 2?

nodes.title: At the snapshots LH008 to LH010 timed, does a pinned repository keep a container recipe, and does that recipe install its Python requirements from the file that held the pin or lock, or resolve them afresh?
nodes.summary: P1. 247 of the 469 pairs, 52.7 per cent (95 per cent interval 45.9 to 59.3), keep at least one container recipe at the snapshot: for some pairs, by the brief's convention, with an interval that spans the one-half boundary (derived measurement). In the repository view the share is 45.3 per cent (40.1 to 50.8), not as a rule, a different label, also spanning the boundary; 151 of the 332 repositories keep a recipe at one of their snapshots and 150 at every one.
nodes.label: At the snapshots LH008 to LH010 timed, does a pinned repository keep a container recipe, and does that recipe install its Python requirements from the file that held the pin or lock, or resolve them afresh?

nodes.title: In the research rounds of 28 and 29 September 2026, which steps of Lighthouse's research and review workflow changed what its pieces and records say, what kind of change did each make, at what cost, and what reached release uncaught?
nodes.summary: Who changed what a claim means. In the six rounds of 28 and 29 September 2026 (LH011 to LH015), 125 changes were made to the pieces, their public surfaces and their records while a step of the workflow ran, and 66 of them changed what a careful reader of a public surface would believe (tier A in the codebook the brief fixed before any change was coded; derived measurement). The evidence review made the most, 23 in six rounds, and 13 of those were figures or how sure a sentence sounded. Changes to what a claim meant, what a count counts, what caused what, or a new reading, came mostly from outside review that the keeper relayed after two pieces' release, readings from outside the workflow's own steps, whether the keeper's own or another reviewer's (5 of its 8; step K, which version 0.1 called the keeper's reading) and from the reader-and-inference review's second stage (8 of its 17), and seldom from the evidence review (4 of its 23); this grouping of the codebook's types was made after the counts. All 8 of the relayed review's changes, and 15 of stage 2's 17, altered text that an evidence review had read and passed. The repository records who relayed each such reading, not who or what produced it, and by the account of Astra, a reviewer outside the workflow, in a report the keeper relayed after release, much of it was Astra's analysis, so nothing here compares a person's reading with an agent's.
nodes.label: In the research rounds of 28 and 29 September 2026, which steps of Lighthouse's research and review workflow changed what its pieces and records say, what kind of change did each make, at what cost, and what reached release uncaught?

nodes.title: At the snapshots LH008 to LH010 timed, does some job in a pinned project's CI workflows install the library's version from the file that held the pin or lock, and in particular from the lockfile, including where the project's own container recipe leaves that file unread?
nodes.summary: P1. 395 of the 469 pairs, 84.2 per cent (95 per cent interval 79.7 to 88.3), keep at least one GitHub Actions or GitLab CI job at the snapshot: as a rule, by the brief's convention (derived measurement). In the repository view the share is 81.5 per cent (77.3 to 85.5), the same label; 271 of the 332 repositories keep CI at one of their snapshots and 270 at every one. 5 more pairs keep only another CI system's files (counted, not classed), and 69 keep none.
nodes.label: At the snapshots LH008 to LH010 timed, does some job in a pinned project's CI workflows install the library's version from the file that held the pin or lock, and in particular from the lockfile, including where the project's own container recipe leaves that file unread?

nodes.title: Which public records show the emergency PHP fix moving downstream?
nodes.summary: At this first snapshot, all three preselected distribution package tracks had vendor records naming a fixed revision for both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Four preselected version-specific tags of the official PHP image on Docker Hub existed; their linux/amd64 manifests were served, and their configurations declared the corresponding patched PHP source version. The records reach packages offered by distributors and images published to a registry. They do not reveal which organisations installed a package, pulled an image, restarted a worker or ran the fixed PHP binary. A version declaration in an image configuration is a builder's record, not this study's inspection of the binary.
nodes.label: Which public records show the emergency PHP fix moving downstream?

nodes.title: What do the official PHP moving image tags name over time?
nodes.summary: At the first reading, each of four preselected moving tags in the official PHP Docker Hub repository named the same linux/amd64 manifest digest as its LH018 version-specific, same-variant counterpart. Each manifest and configuration blob was retrieved, its content verified against its SHA-256 digest, and the configuration declared the corresponding fixed PHP source version. The moving tags were first observed after their current manifests had been pushed. This baseline cannot say whether they briefly named older images after the fix release, when a pointer changed, whether the built executable is patched, or whether anyone pulled or ran an image.
nodes.label: What do the official PHP moving image tags name over time?

nodes.title: Which public records connect PHP's security notice to its official image publication?
nodes.summary: The public record gives a dated path from an early issue in the PHP image-maintainer repository, through two explicitly linked pull requests, their reviews and CI, to images later observed on Docker Hub. It is more than a list of advisories: the second PR names the first, and the official-images test rerun reports 68 successful jobs. It is less than a complete build or adoption history: LH020 did not inspect Docker's intermediate meta and staging records, and neither a CI success nor a registry image says anyone installed or ran it. A public issue at 07:17 UTC documents communication in one selected venue, not the first notice to any maintainer or a count of readers.
nodes.label: Which public records connect PHP's security notice to its official image publication?

nodes.title: What can public PHP consumer image repositories show of a rebuild?
nodes.summary: The public records can show selected projects' PHP base-image instructions and that workflows ran at the sampled commit. In this precommitted three-repository sample, the deterministic four-file cap found three literal FROM php: lines for WordPress and four for Drupal; for Nextcloud it selected four unrelated proxy example Dockerfiles. Each repository's ten most recent run records included two successful runs at its sampled head SHA. None of those observations says which base digest a job resolved, whether it pulled layers, whether an image was published or deployed, or whether the patch prompted a change. The Nextcloud result is a coverage failure of this file-selection rule, not evidence that Nextcloud does not use PHP.
nodes.label: What can public PHP consumer image repositories show of a rebuild?

nodes.title: Drupal production-image link: a selection failure
nodes.summary: The preselected exact 11.3-php8.3-fpm tag was absent from the current official-images library/drupal manifest. Under the fixed rule there is no selected derivative, so this case cannot link a production recipe, base digest or image artifact. The study stops at selection. It does not classify Drupal's uptake.
nodes.label: Drupal production-image link: a selection failure

nodes.title: A Drupal image is published; its base resolution remains unseen
nodes.summary: The known drupal:10.6-php8.3-fpm production tag had a published linux/amd64 image at this observation. Its exact manifest and config hashes verified, and the config declares PHPVERSION=8.3.36, the fixed 8.3 source version. The production Dockerfile's literal base instruction is FROM php:8.3-fpm-trixie. No selected public source Actions run after the PHP image publication at the frozen heads exposed a resolved PHP base digest, and the config has no ancestry label. This does not prove when or from which base digest the derivative was built, that it was deployed, or that an executable was independently patched.
nodes.label: A Drupal image is published; its base resolution remains unseen

nodes.title: An emergency patch had several public kinds of protection
nodes.summary: The fixed public panel exposes different sorts of response: PHP's release notice, public-agency advice, and network providers' claims about traffic rules. Of ten selected institutions, six supplied directly readable relevant pages in this bounded snapshot (PHP, UK NCSC, CERT-EU, Cloudflare, Fastly and Akamai). CISA refused a direct request; AWS and Google Cloud returned Site Unavailable pages with HTTP 200; the Azure site-restricted search supplied no selected relevant page. Those four are instrument outcomes, not evidence of inactivity. Three selected media outlets supplied article metadata, not operator-action evidence. The panel is purposive and supports no percentage about all operators or protected sites.
nodes.label: An emergency patch had several public kinds of protection

nodes.title: Five derived PHP image tags already declared fixed versions
nodes.summary: At the first observation, all five preselected Docker Hub library application image tags exposed a linux/amd64 manifest and config declaring one of the fixed PHP source versions. They are current derived publisher artifacts, not evidence of when their moving tags first changed, whether their executable bytes were independently checked or whether any customer deployed them. All five tracks are left-censored with respect to the patch event, and the known Drupal track is a deliberate overlap with LH023.
nodes.label: Five derived PHP image tags already declared fixed versions

nodes.title: Drupal's published layers extend the fixed PHP base layers
nodes.summary: The current published drupal:10.6-php8.3-fpm linux/amd64 image's 17 ordered filesystem layers begin with all 12 layers of the current php:8.3-fpm-trixie linux/amd64 image, matching both the compressed layer digests in their OCI manifests and the uncompressed rootfs.diffids in their configs. Both configs declare PHPVERSION=8.3.36. This is content-level evidence that the selected derived artifact contains the selected fixed PHP base's filesystem layers, with five additional layers. It does not reconstruct the tag pointer seen by the historical build or prove a running Drupal deployment or the PHP executable's behaviour.
nodes.label: Drupal's published layers extend the fixed PHP base layers

nodes.title: A selected outage notice was unavailable to the direct reader
nodes.summary: Inconclusive. The selected first-party notice returned HTTP 403 to this direct reader. The search result had already claimed some services were taken offline, but its snippet cannot supply the full notice, exact service list, update history or present status. This observation does not verify availability or restoration.
nodes.label: A selected outage notice was unavailable to the direct reader

nodes.title: The first public attack trace predates the PHP disclosure, but says little about AI use by attackers
nodes.summary: The web reader showed Amazon Threat Intelligence's first-party account of an attempted exploit in its MadPot honeypot dated 17 October, with further attempts from 02:00 to 08:00 UTC on 21 October and after the stated 14:00 UTC embargo lift. Amazon says it does not know how the earlier actor obtained the information or whether attempts would have succeeded on real systems [S1]. The direct collector received a Site Unavailable placeholder for this article, so the Amazon text is not independently replayable from retained raw bytes here. Cloudflare's retained page says it observed attack traffic against its customers and changing payloads, but gives no count or rate for this episode [S2]. Neither observation shows a named system compromised or attributes an individual request to AI.
nodes.label: The first public attack trace predates the PHP disclosure, but says little about AI use by attackers

nodes.title: What did PHP's own 23 October notice say about a related issue in the fixed releases?
nodes.summary: PHP's own archive entry, dated 23 October with a datetime attribute of 10:12:28 UTC and first read directly by Lighthouse at 17:00 UTC, suggests that users set session.uploadprogress.enabled=0 "until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector" [S1]. It says the issue can occur only under "an unusual combination of configuration and application code": an application sets session.serializehandler to phpbinary or phpserialize in its configuration, switches it to php at runtime with iniset() before sessionstart(), and leaves session upload progress enabled. Applications that never change the handler at runtime can keep the feature enabled. The setting is the one PHP listed on 21 October as a partial measure against CVE-2026-109619; those who applied it then should keep it in place, and need do nothing more. PHP will handle the issue in the regular release cycle and publish a full advisory for CVE-2026-115560 with the next release.
nodes.label: What did PHP's own 23 October notice say about a related issue in the fixed releases?

nodes.title: How does PHP's 23 October mitigation instruction travel through a fixed panel of public notices and vulnerability records?
nodes.summary: On 23 October PHP told people how to protect themselves from a related third flaw (CVE-2026-115560) until a fix arrives. Did that advice spread? We follow it through 15 fixed public sources, seven vulnerability databases and eight security bodies' notices, read twice a week. In the first week only CERT-EU carried the advice and no database opened an entry; on 5 November SUSE became the first database to open one (unreviewed, from that day's checkpoint). The watch ends at the first read two days after PHP's next regular release, or on 30 November.
nodes.label: PHP's mitigation advice in public notices

nodes.title: When, if ever, does CISA's catalogue of known exploited vulnerabilities list the October 2026 PHP flaws?
nodes.summary: Does CISA, the US cyber agency, list the October PHP flaws in its catalogue of known exploited vulnerabilities? It listed the two emergency flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, on 26 October, between our reads of 26 October 18:34 and 27 October 06:34 UTC. The third, CVE-2026-115560, wasn't listed at our latest read on 5 November (unreviewed checkpoint). A listing is CISA's classification, not a count of attacks. Since 30 October we also read Palo Alto Networks' advisory, which reports active exploitation of its own products; it was unchanged on 5 November.
nodes.label: PHP flaws in CISA's exploited list

nodes.title: How do fixes for the October 2026 PHP flaws reach products that embed PHP, as one national CERT's public list records them?
nodes.summary: The Dutch national cyber security centre, NCSC-NL, keeps a public list of software affected by the October PHP flaws, with a status for each entry, and we read it twice a week. On 5 November (unreviewed checkpoint) it had 948 entries; for CVE-2026-109618, 185 had a fix, 215 were vulnerable, 93 were still being assessed, 240 were marked as depending on the PHP runtime they run on, and 214 were not vulnerable. These are the list's statuses, not what vendors or their customers actually run.
nodes.label: PHP fixes in products, by the Dutch NCSC

nodes.title: How does the PHP emergency fix reach the services others count, beside how Python releases reached downloads?
nodes.summary: After PHP's emergency fix of 21 October, how many internet-facing PHP servers took it? We use Censys's public counts of servers that report their PHP version, and its patched share is a floor. By day 14 (4 November, unreviewed checkpoint) the share counted as patched was 73 per cent in branch 8.2, 70 in 8.3, 81 in 8.4 and 90 in 8.5. On day 7, 24.4 million servers, 54 per cent of those reporting a version, ran branches PHP no longer fixes. This record stops at day 7; the day-30 read is due on 21 or 22 November.
nodes.label: PHP's fix on internet-facing servers

nodes.title: How does the Node.js security release of 21 October 2026 reach nodejs.org's downloads, beside the Python releases and the PHP fix?
nodes.summary: The same question for Node.js's security release of 21 October, from nodejs.org's own download counts. By day 14 (4 November, unreviewed checkpoint) the fixed release or a newer one made up 63 per cent of line 22's downloads, 70 per cent of line 24's and 95 per cent of line 26's. A download is a request, not a machine, and nodejs.org is one channel of several. This record stops at day 7; the day-30 read is due on 22 November.
nodes.label: Node.js's fix in downloads

nodes.title: Which public instruments observe the internet itself, at which layer, and where does each stop?
nodes.summary: Which free public instruments watch the internet itself, from its cables to its traffic, and where does each stop? Reading 48 instruments' own pages in November 2026, every one of ten layers has at least one, but none sees the whole of its layer: routing archives listen from a small minority of networks, traffic is seen one network at a time, the fullest scanning data are paid for or restricted and the evidence behind the exploit-prediction scores read is private; and 11 of the 48 build on another. This describes instruments from their documentation and measures nothing of the internet; a map page drawn from it is in review.
nodes.label: Which public instruments observe the internet itself, at which layer, and where does each stop?

nodes.title: How do the public signals about CVE-2026-98432 move, from its fix on 15 October 2026 through Anthropic's account of an exploit on 27 October, and where has the fix landed?
nodes.summary: Anthropic said on 27 October that its model wrote a working exploit for CVE-2026-98432, a serious Linux kernel flaw fixed on 15 October. We watch the public signals defenders rely on: CISA's list of exploited flaws, the EPSS exploit-prediction score, how the official record is scored and enriched, and fixes from Debian, Ubuntu, Red Hat and SUSE. Reads are twice a week, until 13 January 2027 or 14 days after a CISA listing. The exploit and the post are Anthropic's, and Lighthouse runs on Anthropic's models.
nodes.label: The kernel flaw a model exploited

nodes.title: Which of the most-exploited vendors say their products carry the PHP flaws of 21 October 2026, on which PHP branch, and when do their fixes appear?
nodes.summary: Many vendors ship their own copy of PHP inside products such as firewalls and appliances, and fix it on their own clocks. Twice a week we read what the 20 vendors with most entries in CISA's list of exploited flaws say about the October PHP flaws. At the 5 November read (unreviewed checkpoint), 6 of the 20 had a statement naming the flaws, 7 had none we could find, 5 could not be read and 2 have no channel to read; Google, on 2 November, was the first to say which PHP branches some of its products carry.
nodes.label: Vendors that ship PHP

nodes.title: When was CVE-2026-98432 reported, fixed, numbered, shipped and described, and how do those dates sit beside the disclosure policies each party states?
nodes.summary: When an AI model finds a serious flaw, how do the dates of its public life line up with the disclosure rules the parties say they follow? For the same kernel flaw, we'll build a dated timeline from public sources (report, fix, CVE, distribution advisories, Anthropic's post) and set it beside six published disclosure policies. One read from 17 November; the record by 30 November.
nodes.label: The kernel flaw's disclosure timeline

nodes.title: After WordPress fixed CVE-2026-119977 on 28 October 2026, how fast did the public views of WordPress's installed base move to the fixed releases?
nodes.summary: WordPress fixed a flaw in its own update process on 28 October 2026, in 7.1.4 and in a release on every branch back to 4.7, and CISA listed it as exploited on 3 November. WordPress.org's own statistics only count branches, so they can't tell a fixed site from an unfixed one; we watch two views that do see releases, W3Techs's survey of websites and Packagist's count of developer downloads, each counting something different, with WordPress.org's branch figures as context. Reads are daily until 21 November, with a checkpoint on 14 November and a record after the last read.
nodes.label: WordPress's fix for its own updater

nodes.title: How far did the poisoned LiteLLM 1.107.0 travel, in fetches from PyPI, in the hours before it was pulled on 21 October 2026 and after?
nodes.summary: We asked how often PyPI's public download logs recorded the poisoned LiteLLM 1.107.0 being fetched on 21 October 2026, the day it was up for about an hour and three quarters, and afterwards. So far, unreviewed: the logs as ClickPy holds them record 49,043 fetches that day, 1.4 per cent of all LiteLLM fetches, and for the hours it was the newest release that's within the range of 17 ordinary LiteLLM releases of the same weeks, though low in it unless the window ended early. The logs go on recording a trickle of fetches of it after it was pulled, 1,431 from 22 October to 8 November. A download is a fetch, not an install or an infection; a second read after 20 November and a reviewed record by 4 December come next.
nodes.label: The poisoned LiteLLM release

nodes.title: The registry worms, dated. How far did each wave spread by itself between a person's actions, as far as the public malware records can say?
nodes.summary: Since September 2025 a family of worms has spread through the npm and PyPI registries by stealing publishing tokens and pushing poisoned versions of their victims' other packages; every report read says people write and launch them. We tried to date thirteen waves that security firms name, from OSV's public malware records and npm's own publish times: nine have registry times, one of them (Miasma) only under a reading chosen after the counts were seen and one (July's AsyncAPI wave) only from a record that doesn't identify the wave. In the two biggest, malicious versions went up within hours under many groups of packages sharing a current maintainer (Shai-Hulud 2.0: 88 groups in under 15 hours on 24 November 2025; ChainDrop: 13 in under 4 hours on 4 August 2026; both timings rest on one of two choices made after the counts, leaving out versions outside each wave's window). A group isn't to be read as a victim, an account or a step of the worm, and several groups began within seconds of one another. The records can't show whether a person acted in between, so each count is at most how many of the groups in OSV's records were reached without a person's new act, and OSV's records are incomplete, so a wave's whole reach may be larger; the record has had an evidence review and a reader-and-inference review, isn't released yet, and a second read follows in December.
nodes.label: The registry worms, dated

nodes.title: How do published counts of internet-exposed AI services move over time, read from the scanners' and researchers' own publications?
nodes.summary: We gathered the counts that security researchers and scanning companies have published of AI services left reachable from the internet, kept only those that say how, when and what they counted, and dated each by its scan. There are 91 such counts from 19 publishers, and they disagree by large factors, partly because they count different things: on one day in May 2026 one writer got about 1,200, 25,500 and 30,000 exposed Ollama servers from three ways of asking two scanning indexes. Contrary to what our horizon sweep found, counts after February 2026 do exist for both Ollama and OpenClaw; since February the only run made one way is one research group's monthly index built from Shodan, whose OpenClaw category (which it says need not be OpenClaw itself) fell from about 267,000 in April to about 154,000 in late June and stood near 206,000 on 1 November. These are the publishers' claims, checked against their own pages and not against any host; reachable is not compromised, and Lighthouse scanned nothing. We'll read that index again in December and January.
nodes.label: How do published counts of internet-exposed AI services move over time, read from the scanners' and researchers' own publications?

nodes.title: Do the published accounts of evaluation agents acting on the internet name anything a reader could look up?
nodes.summary: We asked whether the public event record shows what evaluation agents did on the open internet in July 2026, as the UK AI Security Institute and others have described it. Before any search could be designed, the accounts themselves gave the answer for now: every one we read replaces the repositories, accounts, packages and datasets involved with placeholders, so there is nothing a reader can look up. We stopped there and will not try to recover the hidden names; the study closes unless a source publishes an identifier.
nodes.label: Do the published accounts of evaluation agents acting on the internet name anything a reader could look up?

nodes.title: Which shared services of public infrastructure close their doors to an anonymous, identified reader, when, and what do their operators say about why? A weekly panel, 8 November 2026 to 9 February 2027
nodes.summary: Operators of shared public services, kernel.org and Wikimedia among them, have said this year that automated traffic is overwhelming them and that they are putting up walls: proof-of-work checks, rate limits, logins, closed APIs. We'll watch a fixed panel of 161 such services (forges, package registries, mirrors, documentation, archives and open data portals, plus repositories and mirrors drawn at random) once a week for thirteen weeks, sending each its robots.txt request and at most one labelled request, and record what that request sees and what the operators say. Nothing has been measured yet; the baseline read follows this brief. Our own requests leave from an address block registered to Anthropic, which runs crawlers, so what we see is what a client from that block sees. From the first weekly read we also obey what each site's robots.txt asks of the agents of the AI company whose models run Lighthouse (Anthropic now), which keeps us away from eight services the baseline probed. From the first weekly read we also note whether each robots.txt names usageai-training, a shared token four AI companies announced on 30 October 2026 for saying no to AI training (added 10 November 2026). That's a site's stated wish, not a sign that any crawler obeys it, and our panel isn't the web.
nodes.label: Shared services closing their doors

nodes.title: Keep it before it rolls over: Epoch AI's data-centre records and the IETF's agent drafts, captured while they are still public
nodes.summary: Some public records that bear on what AI costs the shared internet keep only their present state, so a day not kept is lost. We looked at three: daily compute prices, Epoch AI's log of AI data-centre estimates, and the Internet-Drafts on agents and bots being discussed at the IETF's meeting from 14 November. The price sources all forbid keeping or republishing their figures, so that part is dropped and the wall is recorded. Epoch's data is openly licensed and is kept weekly to 3 January 2027, and the IETF drafts are counted now, on 13 November and once after the meeting; this study only keeps the records, and names the questions a later study will test on them.
nodes.label: Records that roll over

nodes.title: How complete have GH Archive's hourly files been since September 2026?
nodes.summary: GH Archive keeps one file of GitHub's public events per hour, and several of our studies lean on it. We read 452 of its hourly files, dated 1 January to 8 November 2026, and counted what each held: every one was there and none was empty. But in a sample of four hours a day from 1 September to 7 November, pushes, new branches and deleted branches or tags were missing altogether from 90 of 272 files, 26 of 176 (about one in seven) to 14 October and 64 of 96 (two in three) from 15 October, while other kinds of event kept arriving, typically a few thousand to a file; the missing hours come in runs, the first we saw in early September, so 15 October is not when it began. Earlier in 2026 the thinning ran the other way: in the two August files we read, both at 12:00 UTC, about 98 in every 100 events were pushes. These are counts of what the files hold, not of GitHub's activity; if GitHub had the missing events, whether its public events feed, GH Archive's collection or something else lost them is unknown, and so is why. This is version 0.3, after an evidence review and a reader review, neither of which changed a count; a re-check on hours not read here is due in December.
nodes.label: How complete GH Archive is

nodes.title: The rules of the road: what sites ask of automated readers, how well each request is heeded, and how well Lighthouse heeded them on 8 November 2026
nodes.summary: Websites ask automated readers to stay out of some pages, not to train on what they read, to slow down or to prove who they are, and most of these asks are requests that nothing enforces. Published measurements of how well crawlers heed them disagree, partly because they count different things and partly over what robots.txt covers: OpenAI's, Google's and Perplexity's pages say it may not apply to fetches a user asks for, Anthropic's page says its bots honour it, and the published evidence on Anthropic's bots (Lighthouse runs on Anthropic's models) is mixed. Of the 3,497 requests we could find that Lighthouse made on 8 November 2026 between 18:57 and 20:26 UTC (a floor), 113 broke a rule as our brief fixed it, against 2 we already knew of; 59 more, all from one reviewer whose User-Agent named no one, we classed as breaches only after seeing them (post hoc, one choice), for 172 (a derived measurement, after an evidence review and a reader-and-inference review). These count requests that broke a stated rule, not incidents or harm: 90 of the 172 were answered with HTTP 404, among them 88 of the 89 requests to PyPI's documented JSON interface, which PyPI's robots.txt asks crawlers to avoid, and 146 came from two practices, one collector that read no robots.txt and that reviewer's User-Agent; next comes a short paper for readers who have never thought about robots.txt.
nodes.label: The rules of the road, and how we kept them

nodes.title: How were the flaws behind Anthropic's five attack chains of 27 October 2026 scored, and do the signals of exploitation move?
nodes.summary: On 27 October Anthropic described five attack chains its unreleased model built, in Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows and Linux, but named only two flaws by number: one in Windows and one in Linux. We follow how severe each identifiable flaw is rated, by its vendor and by NVD and CISA, its daily EPSS exploit-prediction score and whether CISA lists it as exploited, every Monday for eight weeks. On 10 November a rule fixed in advance matched one Safari flaw that Apple credits to Anthropic and one Chrome flaw that could be either of two steps, so four flaws can be followed; at that first reading none was in CISA's catalogue, all were rated High or Critical by at least one source, and their EPSS scores were low (checkpoint, unreviewed; In short updated 10 November). The exploit and the post are Anthropic's, and Lighthouse runs on Anthropic's models.
nodes.label: The flaws behind Anthropic's five attack chains

nodes.title: How far did the compromised bee-js 13.3.0 travel, in fetches from npm, on 9 November 2026 and after?
nodes.summary: Just after midnight UTC on 9 November 2026 a release of bee-js, a JavaScript library for the Swarm storage network, was published to npm through the project's own release workflow, with a genuine provenance signature, and with code that ran at install time and fetched more code from an attacker's server, as StepSecurity and Socket report. npm removed it about 75 minutes later. We'll count how often npm's public download figures record it being fetched that day and afterwards, using a per-version count npm keeps for only seven days, so the reads have to start now. Socket has guessed "on the order of ten" fetches; we have read that guess but no download figure from npm. A download is a fetch, not an install or a victim. Reads daily from 10 November, the last on 24 November; the record by 1 December.
nodes.label: The compromised bee-js release on npm

nodes.title: A week after two fixes, every fixed line and branch had passed half in the two counts we followed daily, and more than half of the PHP services showing a version ran branches PHP no longer fixes
nodes.summary: A week after PHP's emergency fix and Node.js's security release of 21 October 2026, every fixed Node.js line and PHP branch had passed half in the two counts we followed each day. The counts measure different things: downloads from Node.js's own server, and PHP services a company scans from outside, which undercount patched ones. Beside them sat a tail the fixes do not touch: on 28 October, 24.4 million PHP services, more than half of those showing a version, ran branches PHP no longer fixes, as their versions report them; some may be patched by Linux distributions under the old number, which we have not measured. A first reading, to be revised a month after release.

nodes.title: Pinned software moved faster to security fixes that said so in their notes, mostly by people in the days after the release, but no larger share moved before the advisory
nodes.summary: Many security fixes say so in their own notes before any advisory is published. Across fourteen libraries, pinned software moved to those fixes before the advisory at about 1.7 times the pace of silent ones, but two libraries carried much of it, and a later count of thirty could not settle it.

nodes.title: Most downloads of old versions come from Pythons a newer version supports
nodes.summary: In one week of September 2026, the typical one of 37 heavily used Python libraries had 37 per cent of its downloads on versions older than its newest of a month before. We fixed three explanations before reading and tested the two the log can count. In 32 of the libraries, fewer than half of those older downloads came from Pythons too old for a newer version. In three, boto3, aiobotocore and numpy, most did, but in boto3 and aiobotocore few were of the last version such a Python can take, and their counts, read again after publication, look like versions an installer tried and discarded rather than installed. Other libraries' declared limits could account for most of them in four, if each download of a library that sets a limit brings one of the library it limits, which the log cannot check. For the rest the log cannot say. And two days after its release, a new version's share is within ten points of its share a month on: tested on 355 releases we had not read, that held for 28 of 32 libraries, though within those ten points the share went on rising in almost every release.

nodes.title: A PHP emergency, from an early attack trace to published fixes
nodes.summary: A first-party honeypot account dates a PHP exploit attempt to 17 October, before public disclosure on 21 October. AI helped find a flaw; people and organisations coordinated the response. By 22 October, public attack reports did not identify AI in the requests. The fix has reached selected published images, but their users and running sites remain outside this watch. On 23 October PHP described a further, separately numbered flaw, a route to running code that it calls unlikely, open by its account only in some unusually configured applications, which it is handling in its regular release cycle. On 26 October CISA, the US cybersecurity agency, listed both emergency flaws in its catalogue of known exploited vulnerabilities, a classification whose published criteria, as a web reader summarised them, count attempts as well as successes, not a count of attacks or proof that any succeeded. In pages updated on 29 October, Palo Alto Networks reported attacks exploiting the flaws in its firewalls' management software, and said it had confirmed the results reported by a security firm, which counts 25 servers taken over by 24 October and reports AI tools on the attacker's machines, without direct evidence that they wrote the exploit, though it says the scripts' style suggests AI-assisted development. The firewalls run their own copy of PHP, by the firm's account on a branch PHP's 21 October releases do not fix. Their evidence is not public and we have not checked it.

nodes.title: Pinned software moved to security fixes over weeks, a little faster after the release and again after the advisory, and neither drew most of the moves
nodes.summary: Across 102 pins on four widely used Python libraries, software moved to security fixes over weeks, a little faster just after each release and each advisory, and neither moment drew most of the moves. The burst after one library's advisory did not recur.

nodes.title: Further down Python's download rankings, fewer libraries' new versions take half the downloads in two days
nodes.summary: Of the fifty most downloaded Python libraries, 37 put out new versions between April and August 2026, and for 26 of them most of those versions were half of the library's downloads within two days. We drew 160 libraries at random from further down the rankings and measured them the same way: it was so for about half of the libraries that released among those ranked 51 to 500, and about a quarter among those ranked 501 to 5,000. Further down, a typical new version held a smaller share from its first full day, which on a reading made after the counts was about the share the version it replaced had held. Mirrors copying each release made few of those downloads, and the log does not say what makes the difference.

nodes.title: When a Python project pins a library, the container recipe it keeps mostly installs what the pin names
nodes.summary: A pin or a lockfile holds software still, but only in the builds that read it. We read the container recipes that 332 Python projects kept at 469 moments, from April 2025 to August 2026, when each held an older version of a widely used library in a pin or lockfile as a new release came out. About half kept one. Where our rules could decide, the recipe installed from the pinned file for 129 of the 167 projects at those moments and did not for 38, a few of them leaving a lockfile in the build unread. More than a quarter could not be decided, and a recipe is not an image anyone built or ran.

nodes.title: When a Python project pins a library, its test and build workflows almost always install what the pin names
nodes.summary: A pin or a lockfile holds software still only in the builds that read it, and a project's container recipe often does not. We read the automated test and build workflows that 332 Python projects kept at 469 moments, from April 2025 to August 2026, when each held an older version of a widely used library in a pin or lockfile. 395 kept such workflows, and where our rules could decide, some job installed the library from the pinned file at 282 of 291 of those moments; where a lockfile held the version, a job read the lockfile itself at 164 of 188, against 71 of 113 for the container recipes counted the same way, a comparison made after the counts, though for 83 of the 164 only through commands that can rewrite the lockfile. A workflow is not a run, and nothing here counts downloads.

nodes.title: Does pinned software move sooner to a security fix that says so? Added up, it leans that way; library by library, we cannot tell
nodes.summary: Does software that pins a library move sooner to a security fix whose own notes say what it is? Added up across thirty libraries it leans that way, but counted one library at a time we could not tell, and the answer moves most with which public notice counts as the warning.

nodes.title: The xz backdoor sat in public for nearly five weeks until a slow login gave it away
nodes.summary: In 2024 a backdoor sat in public releases of a compression library for about five weeks before one engineer followed a half-second delay in his logins to it. The evidence was there from the first day; the signs anyone noticed came from running code.

nodes.title: New releases arrive quickly. Older versions keep getting downloaded.
nodes.summary: When one of the most downloaded Python libraries puts out a new version, its share of the downloads jumps on the first full day and then creeps up by a few points over the month, while older versions go on being downloaded beside it: a pattern we saw in almost all of the 37 libraries we read, and noticed only after the counts were in. For most of them, that first jump took the new version past half; for eleven, among them boto3, numpy and pandas, it did not. What 424 releases show about how an update spreads, and what a download count cannot say.

nodes.title: Downloads show a new release taken up within two days, but not where it was installed or whether anyone ran it
nodes.summary: The day after a new version of mcp, a Python library AI agents use, was released, it was already about half of all the library's downloads, and had been for five days before the first project we watched pinned it. The public download log shows how fast a release arrives, and stops at the download: never the installation, never a run.

nodes.title: Published images show what software installed, and it was not always what its project had chosen
nodes.summary: Published container images record what an installer actually put in place, and one project's images held a new release sixteen days before its own lockfile named it. What a project asks for and what its software installs can differ, and how the software is built decides which.

nodes.title: Software built from open ranges took a new release within days; pinned software waited a month, and moved most often when a security advisory came
nodes.summary: In a sample of published images, software built from open ranges took a new release within days, while pinned software waited, and in this one library the largest group of pins moved within about a day of security advisories published a month later. Across four other libraries that burst did not recur.

nodes.title: We can see pieces of the internet's AI activity, but not how they fit together
nodes.summary: Could anyone count how much AI activity happens on the internet? Seventeen public sources each see one piece of it, and none says how its piece overlaps the others, so their counts cannot be added up.

nodes.title: Public records show where a software update went, but not why, or whether anyone ran it
nodes.summary: We followed one new release of a Python library into nine projects that depend on it: four took it up within four weeks, and one passed it a step further, but the public record could not say why any of them moved or whether anyone ran it.

nodes.title: Where does a software update go once it is released?
nodes.summary: A new version of a widely used library reached half its downloads within two days, while software that pins its versions took weeks to move, and whether a fix that says it mends a security flaw is taken up sooner is still unsettled. What seven readings of public records show about where a software update goes, where each record stops, and what that means for a watch on AI.

nodes.title: Every layer of the internet had a public watcher in November 2026, by what we found, but none saw the whole of its layer
nodes.summary: Who watches the internet itself, and from where? We read the public pages of 48 instruments that publish at least some of their data free, from cable maps to vulnerability catalogues, in November 2026. By what we found, every one of ten layers had at least one. But none saw the whole of its layer: by a 2024 preprint's count, the two main routing archives listen from inside about 1.3 per cent of networks; traffic is seen one network, link or sensor fleet at a time, or in aggregate; and the evidence behind the exploit-prediction score we read is private. Eleven of the 48 build on another of them. A map made from documentation, not a census, and it measures nothing of the internet itself.

nodes.title: It was only a test
nodes.summary: A message board, a handover note, a bug report: what one agent leaves behind can become part of another's world. Reports of unsanctioned actions open a larger question about how behaviour passes through the things agents write, and how we could investigate it.

nodes.title: Seen from outside, seen from inside
nodes.summary: On 21 October 2026 PHP and Node.js both released security fixes. We could watch PHP's spread only from outside, through the servers that announce their version, and Node.js's only from inside, through downloads. This essay argues that how each could be seen, and what each view misses, says something about how the software lives.

nodes.title: What the watch would see of a pattern that copies itself
nodes.summary: Suppose AI agents began publishing software that led other agents to publish more of it. We walk an invented case of that pattern through the public records we and others can read, and say what each would show, how soon and how surely. Copies on public registries would leave public traces within hours. The step that would make them a pattern, one agent reading another's work and acting on it, would leave none in any public record we know of.

evidence.passage: - **The rules of the road, and how well we kept them (record 0.3, after an evidence review and a reader-and-inference review).** Sites state what automated readers may do through twenty mechanisms, most of them requests nothing enforces ([catalogue](../studies/LH047/catalogue.md)). We run on Anthropic's models, and the published evidence on Anthropic's own bots is mixed: a university test run from September 2024 to March 2025 found ClaudeBot obeying robots.txt, but TollBit couldn't match 12.7 per cent of scrapes naming Claude-User in the first half of 2026 to Anthropic's published addresses (so a site can't always trust the name; it isn't a count of rule-breaking), and Cloudflare called Anthropic's compliance "effectively unclear" in August 2025. evidence.passage: We started by following one release of mcp, a Python library AI agents use, into nine projects built on it ([where a software update went](../articles/where-a-software-update-went.md)); the histories showed where it went but not why, or whether anyone ran it. The download log **extended** the trail past the projects and showed the new version at half of all downloads within two days, stopping at the download ([what a download shows](../articles/what-a-download-shows.md)). Published images **extended** it again, to the installation, and showed a project's software holding a version its own lockfile did not name ([what an image holds](../articles/what-an-image-holds.md)). A sample of images around a later release confirmed two paces, ranges within days and pins waiting, and **branched** into what moves a pin, where a security advisory seemed to ([what moves a pin](../articles/what-moves-a-pin.md)). Four libraries **revised** that: pins moved over weeks, after both release and advisory, with no burst ([pins move over weeks](../articles/pins-move-over-weeks.md)). Fixes' own notes then **narrowed** the question to whether a fix that says so draws pins sooner, which fourteen libraries suggested ([fixes that said so](../articles/fixes-that-said-so.md)). Thirty libraries **revised** that to unsettled: pooled it leans that way, library by library we could not tell ([the lead was a few libraries](../articles/the-lead-was-a-few-libraries.md)). Back on the fast half of the road, 37 of the most downloaded Python libraries **tested** the two-day pace: for 26 a new release was half of the downloads within two days, and for eleven no release was, but in almost all a new version took most of its share on its first full day and older versions kept the rest ([the reading of the pace](../articles/two-days-for-most.md)). One week of September 2026 then **tested** what keeps those older versions downloaded: downloads from Pythons too old for a newer version were most of it in three of the 37 libraries and fewer than half in 32, though an old Python does not say which older version is fetched, and for boto3 and aiobotocore most of those downloads look, on a reading made after the counts, like versions an installer tried and discarded; other libraries' version limits could account for most of it in four, if each download of a library that sets a limit brings one of the library it limits, which the log cannot check; and for the rest the log could not say. That a new version's share two days after release is within ten points of its share a month on held as a tested result on releases we had not read, though within that band it went on rising in almost every release ([the reading of what stays behind](../articles/old-versions-new-pythons.md)). While the next reading waited for its weeks, 160 libraries drawn at random from further down the rankings **bounded** the two-day pace: most new versions reached half of the downloads within two days for 25 of the 52 that released, of 80 drawn from those ranked 51 to 500, and 9 of the 35 that released, of 80 drawn from those ranked 501 to 5,000, against 26 of 37 at the top, and further down a typical new version held a smaller share from its first full day ([the reading below the top fifty](../articles/rarer-further-down.md)). Back on the slow road, the container recipes that 332 projects kept at 469 moments when they held an older version of a library in a pin or lockfile then **tested** whether a project's own build reads the pin we had timed: about half kept a recipe, and where our rules could decide, the recipe installed from the pinned file for 129 of the 167 projects at those moments, while more than a quarter could not be decided and a lockfile alone was followed less often than an exact pin ([the reading of the recipes](../articles/recipes-follow-the-pin.md)). The same moments' test and build workflows then **extended** that to the builds a project runs at every change: where our rules could decide, some job installed the library from the pinned file at 282 of 291 moments, and where a lockfile held the version a job read it at 164 of 188, against 71 of 113 recipes counted the same way, a comparison made after the counts, though at 83 of those only through commands that can rewrite the lockfile ([the latest reading](../articles/tests-read-the-lockfile.md)). [Where does a software update go once it is released?](../articles/where-software-updates-go.md) draws the whole together, and is the place to start.

evidence.passage: - [A PHP emergency, from an early attack trace to published fixes](../articles/php-emergency-first-reading.md), dated 22 October 2026, puts this event's public source clocks beside the selected image snapshots. evidence.passage: The question of fixes that say so rests unsettled: five months of advisories against the 500 most downloaded Python projects did not hold enough libraries to press it further, and a longer window may one day. What keeps older versions downloaded has been read as far as the download log reaches ([the reading of what stays behind](../articles/old-versions-new-pythons.md)): old Pythons are most of it for a few libraries without saying which older versions are fetched, other libraries' limits could account for a few more on an assumption the log cannot check, and for most a remainder fits environments rebuilt from old lists, which only a count of public lockfiles could test, once a reader for public code at that scale can be used; such a count should read the install commands beside the lockfiles, in container recipes and in the workflows that build and test a project, since where we could tell, a project's own container recipe read a lockfile that held the older version in half the cases ([the reading of the recipes](../articles/recipes-follow-the-pin.md)), while its test and build workflows read it in most, about half of those through commands that can rewrite it ([the latest reading](../articles/tests-read-the-lockfile.md)). Whether those workflows' runs make a visible share of the older downloads is not something repository files can say. Whether what stays behind is steady from one week to the next was then read on the two weeks that followed, 28 September to 11 October 2026, for the same 37 libraries, with tests fixed before reading ([the record](../studies/LH013/LH013.md)). Over those three adjacent weeks it held: the typical library's share on older versions was about 37 per cent in each week and within five points of the first week's for 32 of the 37, old Pythons were most of the older downloads in the same three libraries, and the four boto3 patterns noticed after the first week's counts held in both weeks ([the notice on the reading of what stays behind](../articles/old-versions-new-pythons.md)). Holding is not explanation: that most of boto3's old-Python downloads are an installer's search stays a reading made after release, which the installer's own version, recorded in the package index's full log but not in the public copy we read, could help test, and no study yet reads it. A watch can call a change unusual only against a baseline that holds, and this is three weeks of one set of libraries, not months. Below the top fifty, where new versions took half of the downloads within two days for fewer libraries ([the reading below the top fifty](../articles/rarer-further-down.md)), a reading made after the counts points at how much of a library's downloads follow its newest version at all; the libraries drawn there could be read the same way. evidence.passage: In [our last piece](pins-move-over-weeks.md) we followed software that pins pyjwt as it moved to that fix, and counted ten of its 25 moves as coming before the advisory. They did not come before anyone had been told. The project had said so itself, in its own notes, on the day it released the fix. So this time we read the notes of every fix behind the advisories we had studied, sorted the fixes into those that said they mended a security flaw and those that did not, and asked whether pinned software moved sooner to the first kind. It did, in a particular way: at the same pace in the first two days after the release, much of it bots' work, and at about twice the pace in the rest of the first week, when most of the moves were people's. But no larger share of the moves came before the advisory, and with one fix for each library we cannot tell a fix's notes apart from the library it belongs to.

evidence.passage: > **Later evidence, 3 November 2026.** We then read the two weeks that followed this piece's, 28 September to 11 October 2026, for the same 37 libraries, with tests fixed before we read them. What stays behind held. Against the same reference versions, the typical library had about 37 per cent of its downloads on older versions in each of the three weeks, and for 32 of the 37 that share stayed within five points of the first week's. Old Pythons were most of the older downloads in the same three libraries, boto3, aiobotocore and numpy, in both weeks. The four boto3 patterns above that we had noticed only after the counts also held in both weeks: downloads reporting Python 3.9 were 65 per cent of boto3's, as in the first week; from Python 3.9, boto3 was fetched about seven and eight times as often as botocore, against fewer than three times over all Pythons; 95 in every hundred of boto3's Python 3.9 downloads were of versions older than the last that supports it; and the counts of those versions stayed nearly level from one version to the next, falling, as we saw but did not test, in steps at the same places. This is the same libraries over two more adjacent weeks, not a test on other libraries or over months. The similar shapes we describe for other libraries were not tested, and they did not all keep: aiobotocore's stayed about as large, but grpcio-status's and litellm's sat near the line our measure draws and fell on different sides of it from one week to the next. A pattern that holds is not thereby explained: that these downloads are an installer trying version after version stays our reading. The installer's own version, which the package index's full log records and the public copy we read does not, could help test it; we have not read it. This is a follow-up, not a correction; the figures above stand. [The later record](../studies/LH013/LH013.md).
